Battle of Tarawa. Fought from November twentieth to twenty-third, nineteen forty-three, the Battle of Tarawa was the first major amphibious assault by American forces against a heavily fortified Japanese atoll in the Central Pacific. The three-day battle to capture the tiny atoll of Betio resulted in a strategic American victory but demonstrated the devastating cost of island assaults, with over one thousand American lives lost and nearly all Japanese defenders killed.

The battle was fought on Betio, a small islet within Tarawa Atoll in the Gilbert Islands. The Japanese garrison of approximately forty-five hundred troops was under Rear Admiral Keiji Shibasaki, while the American landing force of thirty-five thousand Marines of the Second Marine Division was under Major General Julian Smith, in what was called operation Galvanic.

The Japanese position was heavily fortified with concrete blockhouses, anti-tank gun emplacements, barbed wire, and mined beaches that created killing zones. U.S. casualties reached one thousand nine killed and over twenty-one hundred wounded in three days of intense close-quarters combat. Japanese casualties approached total destruction of the garrison. The battle became iconic for the intensity of hand-to-hand fighting amid fortified positions as Marines were forced to clear pillboxes methodically under fire. The Americans achieved dominance in the Central Pacific, opening a direct route toward Japan. The American public was shocked by casualty photographs, which demonstrated that island-hopping would exact a terrible price, a lesson that would only grow more terrible at Saipan and beyond.
